title: Identify basic breeding practices for farm animals

lessons.title: Signs of heat in females and libido in males
lessons.html:
When is the female ready to mate?

A female animal can only fall pregnant at a certain time in her cycle. This time is called heat or oestrus. If you see heat at the right time, more females fall pregnant and the farm gets more calves, lambs, kids and piglets.

Standing heat

The best sign of heat is standing heat. The female stands still when another animal climbs on her back. If she walks away, she is not in standing heat.

Other signs of heat

AnimalSigns
CowStands to be mounted, clear slime from the vulva, red and swollen vulva, restless, bellows, rubbed hair on the tail-head
Ewe and doe goatLooks for the ram or buck, wags the tail (goats), stands for the male; signs are often hard to see without a male
SowRed, swollen vulva, stands very still when you press hard on her back, ears stiff

How to check for heat

  • Watch the females at least twice a day, early morning and late afternoon.
  • Watch for about 20 to 30 minutes each time.
  • Write down the animal's number, the date and the time.
  • Tell your supervisor at once, so the female can be mated or inseminated at the right time.

Is the male keen to mate?

Libido means the male's desire to mate. A bull, ram, buck or boar with good libido looks for females in heat, smells them, and mounts them.

  • Good libido: the male follows females, sniffs and curls his top lip, mounts and serves.
  • Poor libido: the male stands alone, shows no interest, or tries but cannot serve.

A male may have poor libido if he is sick, lame, too thin, too fat, too young or too old. Report this to your supervisor. Bulls should be checked by a vet before the breeding season.

Safety: bulls and boars can be very dangerous. Never go into a camp or pen with a bull alone. Always know where your way out is.

lessons.title: Signs of birth and problems at birth
lessons.html:
The birth is coming

Before birth the female's body changes. Learn these signs so you can watch her closely.

  • The udder gets bigger and full of milk. The teats may leak.
  • The vulva gets soft and swollen.
  • The muscles near the tail-head go soft and sunken.
  • She goes away from the herd and looks for a quiet place.
  • She is restless. She lies down and gets up often.
  • A sow makes a nest with straw.

A normal birth

  1. First the water bag comes out.
  2. Then two front feet appear, with the soles facing down, and the nose lying on the legs.
  3. The female strains and the young animal comes out.
  4. The afterbirth comes out later, usually within some hours.

Most births need no help. Watch quietly from a distance. Do not chase or disturb her.

When something is wrong

Call your supervisor or the vet straight away if you see any of these:

  • She strains hard for a long time and nothing comes out.
  • Only one leg, only the head, or the tail comes out first.
  • The feet come out with the soles facing up. The young animal may be backwards.
  • The young animal is very big and stuck.
  • She is very weak, cannot stand, or is bleeding a lot.
  • The womb comes out behind her (a prolapse).

Never pull hard on a young animal with ropes, a bakkie or a tractor. This can kill both mother and young. Only trained people should help with a difficult birth. Wear gloves and wash your hands and arms well afterwards, because some diseases from birth fluids can make people sick.

lessons.title: Caring for mother and young after birth
lessons.html:
The first hours

The time after birth is called the post-partum period. Watch the mother and the young one closely.

A normal mother

  • She licks the young animal clean and dry.
  • She stays close to it and calls to it.
  • She lets it drink milk.
  • Her afterbirth comes out.
  • She eats and drinks normally within a day.

A normal young animal

  • It breathes well and lifts its head.
  • It stands up soon after birth.
  • It finds the teat and drinks.

The first milk is called colostrum. It is thick and yellow. It protects the young animal from disease. The young animal must drink colostrum as soon as possible after birth.

Signs of trouble

MotherYoung animal
Does not want her young or kicks it awayCannot stand or is very weak
Afterbirth stays inside too longDoes not drink
Bad smell or pus from the vulvaCold, or lying flat
Hot, hard or red udderDiarrhoea
Does not eat, cannot get upSwollen, wet navel

Report any of these to your supervisor at once. Write down the mother's number, the date of birth, and whether the young one is male or female.

Keep the birth camp or pen clean and dry. Move sick animals to a separate pen. Treat animals calmly and gently. Cruelty or neglect is against the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

Key points

  • Standing heat means the female stands still when mounted.
  • Check for heat twice a day and write down what you see.
  • A good male follows, smells and mounts females in heat.
  • Call for help at once if a birth is not normal; never pull hard.
  • The young animal must drink colostrum soon after birth.

quiz.question: What is the best sign that a cow is in heat?

options.text: She stands still when another animal mounts her
She walks away from the herd

quiz.question: How often should you watch females for heat?

options.text: At least twice a day, early morning and late afternoon

quiz.question: In a normal birth, what usually comes out first after the water bag?

options.text: Two front feet with soles facing down and the nose on the legs
The first thick, yellow milk that protects the young animal

quiz.question: What should you do if a female strains hard for a long time and nothing comes out?

options.text: Pull the young out with a bakkie
Leave her alone for two days
Call your supervisor or the vet straight away

A male with poor libido shows little interest in females.

She goes away from the herd to a quiet place
